passage: I'm Jeevan. Alka and I share a desk at the call centre. Last Tuesday our team lead came back from a meeting and snapped at everyone about targets. Most of us muttered and went back to calls. Alka watched him for a while. Later I saw her bring him a cup of tea and ask, quietly, 'Tough meeting?' He sighed and said the whole floor might face cuts. She nodded, didn't push, and told him to let her know if the team could help with anything. The next day he apologised to everyone for being short. I don't know if Alka guessed it or just got lucky. But I noticed she'd been watching his face, not just his words.

qa.q: What did Alka bring the team lead?
qa.a: She brought him a cup of tea.

qa.q: What did Alka seem to guess about her team lead's mood?
qa.a: She seemed to sense that his snapping came from stress, not anger at the team.

qa.q: What could others learn from how Alka handled the team lead?
qa.a: Noticing someone's mood and asking gently in private can calm a situation better than muttering or snapping back.

qa.q: How might the team lead have felt when Alka asked about the meeting?
qa.a: He likely felt some relief that someone noticed he was under pressure rather than just reacting to him. 🙂

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a colleague read her boss's mood and respond thoughtfully.

passage:
Day one: Gurleen texted her flatmate Farida, "Want to watch a film tonight?" Farida replied, "k." Gurleen went to bed thinking Farida was annoyed with her.

Day three: At breakfast Farida seemed quiet, stirring her tea without drinking it. This time Gurleen didn't assume it was about her. She asked, "You okay? You seem far away." Farida admitted her internship had been cancelled and she hadn't told her parents.

Day six: Farida's replies were still short. Gurleen stopped reading them as cold. She left a note on the fridge: "Chai at 7? No talking required 🙂". Farida came, sat, and after a while started talking on her own. Gurleen mostly listened.

qa.q: What did Farida reply when Gurleen suggested a film?
qa.a: She replied, 'k.'

qa.q: What did Gurleen assume on day one, and why?
qa.a: She assumed Farida was annoyed with her because the reply was so short.

qa.q: What changed in how Gurleen responded by day three?
qa.a: She checked instead of assuming, asking gently when she noticed Farida seemed distracted.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Farida during those days?
qa.a: She was carrying bad news she hadn't told her parents, so she likely had little energy for long replies or conversation.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning over several days to read a friend's mood accurately and respond with care.

passage: Avni beta, let me tell you about my first job at the textile mill. I was twenty-two, supervising older workers. One morning my best weaver, Saurabh, was banging his loom and muttering. I nearly scolded him in front of everyone. Instead I noticed he kept looking at the door. At lunch I sat with him and asked about his family. His son had a fever and he'd left him with neighbours. I sent him home early and covered his loom myself. Saurabh never forgot it. Later, when others wanted to strike over a small quarrel, he spoke up to calm them. You see, I didn't read minds. I just watched, and asked before judging. You'll manage people soon. Remember that.

qa.q: What was Saurabh doing that nearly made the storyteller scold him?
qa.a: He was banging his loom and muttering.

qa.q: What clue helped the storyteller guess Saurabh was worried, not rude?
qa.a: He kept looking at the door, which suggested his mind was somewhere else.

qa.q: What lesson is being passed to Avni for managing people?
qa.a: Watch carefully and ask privately before judging someone's mood or behaviour.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt when he was sent home early?
qa.a: He probably felt grateful and understood, which explains why he later helped calm others.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how noticing a worker's mood and responding with care built trust at work.

passage: The Saturday rush at the café in Dharamshala hit at noon, and one server hadn't turned up. Sahil and Dolma were alone behind the counter with a queue out the door. Dolma, usually the one humming and joking with trekkers, was snapping at him: 'Not that cup! Move!' Sahil felt his own temper flare. He noticed, though, that her eyes were red and she kept checking her phone between orders. Instead of snapping back, he said, 'I'll take the till and orders. You just do the coffee.' She nodded without looking at him. The queue moved faster. At three, when it finally slowed, he slid a glass of water towards her. 'Rough day?' She let out a long breath. 'My grandmother's in hospital. I'm sorry I was awful.' 'You weren't. Go call home. I've got this.'

qa.q: Where did Sahil and Dolma work?
qa.a: At a café in Dharamshala.

qa.q: What cues made Sahil think something was wrong with Dolma?
qa.a: Her snapping was unlike her usual humming and joking, her eyes were red and she kept checking her phone.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that helped during the rush?
qa.a: He held back his temper, took the till and orders so she had only one task, and waited for a quiet moment to check in gently.

qa.q: What might Dolma have felt when Sahil slid the water across?
qa.a: Relieved and a little guilty about snapping, which let her finally share what was worrying her.

grounding: Shows a young worker reading a colleague's mood under pressure and responding thoughtfully instead of reacting.

passage: In the Noida office, Monday's stand-up ended with the manager calling Chetan's report 'sloppy' in front of everyone. Chetan said, 'Okay, noted,' and went back to his desk. Saurabh, who sat across from him, noticed the clipped tone, the headphones going on, the lunch box left unopened, one spreadsheet stared at for an hour. Maybe he was just busy, Saurabh thought. Maybe not. He didn't want to make it a big thing in front of others. So at four he messaged: 'Chai downstairs? My treat.' At the tea stall Chetan finally said, 'He could have told me privately.' Saurabh didn't rush to defend the manager or trash him. 'Yeah, that stung, I could tell. Want help going through the report tomorrow?' Chetan's shoulders came down a little. 'Yeah. Thanks, man.'

qa.q: What did the manager call Chetan's report?
qa.a: 'Sloppy', in front of everyone at the stand-up.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh wait until four and message privately?
qa.a: He felt unsure what Chetan was feeling and was cautious not to make it a big thing in front of others.

qa.q: What made Saurabh's response thoughtful?
qa.a: He acknowledged the sting without defending or trashing the manager, and offered practical help with the report.

qa.q: How might the manager's public comment have felt to Chetan?
qa.a: Humiliating; he wished it had been said privately, as he told Saurabh.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing a colleague's mood from small cues and responding with care at the right moment.

passage:
"Morning!" Avni set down two cups of cutting chai. "Got you one."
Anjali didn't look up from her screen. "Thanks."
"You okay? You're typing like the keyboard owes you money."
"I'm fine."
Avni paused. Anjali's jaw was tight, and the steel lunchbox she always brought was missing. "Okay. I'll leave the chai. If you want to walk at lunch, I'm going anyway."
At one o'clock Anjali appeared by her desk. They walked round the building twice before she spoke. "My review. Sir called my work 'adequate'. In front of the whole team."
"Ouch. In front of everyone?"
"I wanted to cry in the washroom."
Avni didn't rush to fix it. "That sounds humiliating."
"It was." Anjali breathed out. "Thanks for not pushing this morning."
"You looked like pushing would have made it worse."

qa.q: What word did Sir use for Anjali's work?
qa.a: Adequate.

qa.q: Why did Avni decide not to push in the morning?
qa.a: Avni sensed Anjali was upset and felt concerned, judging that pushing would only make it worse.

qa.q: What did Avni notice, and how did she respond thoughtfully?
qa.a: The tight jaw, the missing lunchbox and the short replies; she left the chai and a low-pressure offer to walk, then listened without trying to fix it.

qa.q: What was it like for Anjali to be called 'adequate' in front of the team?
qa.a: It felt humiliating; she wanted to cry, and was grateful Avni gave her space before talking.

grounding: At work, a young woman reads a colleague's mood from small cues and responds with space and quiet support.

passage: I, Mahima, used to take every silence personally. If Nitin went quiet on our evening walk, I assumed I'd done something, and I'd poke until we fought. Last month he came back from a call with his father and said, "Let's just walk." Old me would have asked, "Are you angry with me?" ten times. This time I noticed things instead. He was gripping his phone too tightly. He kept looking at the ground. But he didn't let go of my hand, which told me it wasn't about me. So I just walked with him, chatting about nothing: the mango seller, the new dog in our lane. On the second round of the park he said, "Papa's shop is losing money. He sounded scared." I didn't rush to advise. I said, "That's a lot to hear." He nodded, and we kept walking. It's still hard not to make things about me. But I'm getting better at reading before reacting.

qa.q: What did Nitin talk about on the second round of the park?
qa.a: That his Papa's shop is losing money.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Nitin went quiet this time?
qa.a: Mahima felt a flicker of the old anxiety but stayed calm, reassured by the held hand that his mood wasn't about Mahima.

qa.q: How did Mahima respond thoughtfully once Nitin spoke?
qa.a: Mahima didn't rush to advise, simply acknowledged it was a lot to hear, and kept walking with him.

qa.q: What was it like for Nitin after the call with his father?
qa.a: Nitin was worried and upset, and having Mahima just walk beside him gave him space to say it when ready.

grounding: A young adult looks back on learning to read a partner's mood from cues instead of taking silence personally.

passage: Front office supervisor's note, trainee review. Last night at 11 p.m., Mr Abhinav Rao arrived after a cancelled flight to find his room given away. He was loud, red-faced and slapping the counter. Urmila (trainee) was alone at the desk. I watched from the back office. She didn't argue or apologise ten times. She lowered her voice, said, "You've had a terrible day and now this. Let me fix it," and offered him water while she checked options. His shoulders dropped a little. She noticed his hands shaking and asked if he had eaten; he hadn't. She arranged a sandwich from the kitchen and an upgraded room in under ten minutes. He thanked her by name when he left this morning. I have recommended her for guest relations training and will share this at Monday's briefing. — M. Fernandes, supervisor

qa.q: When did Mr Abhinav Rao arrive?
qa.a: At 11 p.m., after a cancelled flight.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling alone at the desk with a shouting guest?
qa.a: Urmila was probably nervous and under pressure, yet calm enough to read what the guest needed.

qa.q: Which signals did Urmila read, and how did she respond?
qa.a: The loud voice, red face and shaking hands; she lowered her voice, named his bad day, offered water and food, and fixed the room fast.

qa.q: How did the evening feel for Mr Rao by the end?
qa.a: He went from angry and exhausted to calmer and cared for, thanking Urmila by name the next morning.

grounding: A supervisor records how a hotel trainee read an angry guest's state and calmed the situation thoughtfully.

passage:
Tuesday, after closing

Manoj bhaiya was off today. Not rude exactly, just short. "Fine." "Do it." No jokes about the milk frother, which he always jokes about. He also counted the cash drawer twice, which he never does.

My first instinct was to think I'd messed up the morning orders. I nearly asked, "Are you angry with me?" But he wasn't looking at me when he talked, he was looking at his phone every few minutes, so I guessed it was probably not about me.

So I didn't push. I just took the dishes without being asked and handled the loud customer at table four myself. Around six I put a cup of ginger tea by the till and said, "No pressure, but if you need to leave early, I can close."

He looked surprised, then said his father was having tests at the hospital. He left at seven. I closed alone. It took forever but I didn't mind.

— Jasleen

qa.q: What did Manoj do with the cash drawer that he never does?
qa.a: He counted the cash drawer twice.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when she first noticed Manoj's short replies?
qa.a: Jasleen felt anxious and a little defensive, worried she had messed up the morning orders.

qa.q: What did Jasleen's response get right?
qa.a: She read the cues before assuming it was about her, didn't push him to explain, and offered practical help that gave him an easy way out.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Jasleen's offer to close?
qa.a: Manoj was surprised and probably relieved and grateful, since he could leave to be with his father without having to ask.

grounding: A young café worker notices a manager's changed tone, checks whether it is about her, and responds with quiet, practical kindness.

passage:
The milk cooperative in Shirol opens at six, and by half past, the queue of farmers stretches to the tamarind tree. Nitin has worked the testing counter for a year. Pallavi, who logs the readings beside him, usually hums while she writes.

Today she doesn't hum. She writes the numbers very neatly and keeps her face turned towards the ledger. When old Shinde kaka jokes about her handwriting, she smiles with only her mouth.

Nitin thinks of asking her right there, then stops; there are twenty farmers listening. Instead he takes over calling out the readings so she only has to write. At the tea break he sits a little apart, not too close, and says, "You seem quiet today. You don't have to tell me anything. I'm around if you want."

Pallavi is silent for a while. Then she says her marriage talks with a family in Sangli fell through yesterday, and the whole village already knows. Nitin just nods and passes her the biscuits.

qa.q: What does Pallavi usually do while she writes the readings?
qa.a: She usually hums while she writes.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's smile "with only her mouth" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is hurt and embarrassed underneath, putting on a polite face in front of the farmers.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's choices helped Pallavi, and why?
qa.a: Waiting for a private moment and taking over the calling-out helped, because it reduced her load and avoided embarrassing her in front of twenty farmers.

qa.q: If you were Pallavi, what would you want from Nitin after she shares the news?
qa.a: Probably just what he did: to be listened to without questions or advice, and not to have the news become more gossip.

grounding: In a village cooperative, a young man notices a colleague's changed mood and responds with privacy, practical help and a gentle offer to listen.

passage:
In São Paulo, Priscila had worked beside Xin on the same project for a year. Xin was usually chatty, sent jokes in the team chat, brought pastries on Fridays.
This week, Xin's replies were one word. "Ok." "Done." The camera stayed off in meetings. On Thursday, Xin snapped at a junior over a small error, then apologised too many times.
Priscila noticed. She didn't mention it in the group chat, and she didn't assume it was about her. She sent a private message: "Hey, you seem a bit off this week. No need to explain. Want to grab coffee, or should I just take the Friday report so you have one less thing?"
An hour later Xin wrote: "Coffee. Thanks for noticing." Over coffee, Xin said a family member was unwell back in Shanghai.
Priscila took the Friday report.

qa.q: What did Xin's replies become this week?
qa.a: One word, like "Ok" and "Done".

qa.q: What does Xin apologising too many times suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Xin felt stressed and on edge, and guilty about snapping.

qa.q: What did Priscila do well in responding to Xin's mood?
qa.a: Priscila reached out privately, didn't pry or take it personally, and offered practical help as well as company.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt after Xin snapped?
qa.a: The junior was probably hurt and confused, since Xin was usually friendly.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult noticing a colleague's change in tone and mood and responding thoughtfully.

passage:
In the college library's group study room, Ankita's project group was dividing tasks. Charu kept saying "fine" and "whatever works" with a bright smile, but her leg was bouncing under the table and she hadn't opened her laptop.
The others moved on. Ankita noticed. When Charu got up for water, Ankita followed.
"You okay? You're saying fine a lot."
Charu laughed, too quickly. Then her face dropped. "I got the internship rejection this morning. I didn't want to bring the group down."
Ankita didn't give a speech. "That's rough. Do you want a lighter part today?"
Charu thought. "Maybe the references section. I can do that without thinking."
Back in the room, Ankita said casually, "Charu and I swapped." No one asked why. By the end, Charu was cracking jokes again.

qa.q: What did Charu keep saying?
qa.a: "Fine" and "whatever works".

qa.q: How could Ankita tell Charu felt upset despite saying fine?
qa.a: Ankita noticed the bright smile didn't match Charu's bouncing leg and closed laptop, which suggested she felt upset or anxious.

qa.q: What made Ankita's response thoughtful?
qa.a: Ankita checked privately, didn't lecture, offered a practical lighter task, and covered the swap casually so Charu wasn't exposed.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ankita had asked in front of the group?
qa.a: Charu might have felt embarrassed and forced to explain, and could have hidden her feelings even more.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a friend's masked mood during group work and responding sensitively.

passage:
Hafsa,
I've been thinking about Saturday, and I want to say sorry properly, not in a text.
When you came to dinner, you were quiet and kept checking your phone. I thought you were bored with me, and I got sulky and made that comment about "better things to do". I didn't ask what was wrong.
Your sister's call later made it clear: your grandmother was in hospital, and you were waiting for news. You came anyway, because you'd promised.
I read your mood as being about me. Next time I see you go quiet like that, I'll ask, "Is something going on?" before I decide what it means.
How is your grandmother today? If you want, I can come with you to the hospital on Sunday, or I can just bring food and stay out of the way.
Shankar

qa.q: Why was Hafsa checking the phone at dinner?
qa.a: Hafsa's grandmother was in hospital, and Hafsa was waiting for news.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel during the dinner, and how does Shankar see that now?
qa.a: Shankar felt hurt and sulky, thinking Hafsa was bored, and now feels sorry for misreading Hafsa.

qa.q: What will Shankar do differently next time, and why does it help?
qa.a: Shankar will ask "Is something going on?" before deciding what a quiet mood means, because it stops Shankar making Hafsa's feelings about Shankar.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel understood and cared for, and relieved that Shankar sees what was really happening.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult reflecting on misreading a partner's mood and planning to respond more thoughtfully.

passage: Binita, you asked what I meant about reading the room at work, so here's Friday. My manager walked in from a call, dropped her laptop on the desk harder than usual, and said "Fine" when nobody had asked anything. Two months ago I would have jumped in with my weekly report right then, because that was the plan. This time I noticed her jaw, the short answers, the way she didn't sit down. So I waited. I sent a one-line message instead: "Report's ready whenever suits you, no rush today." An hour later she came over, calmer, and said the call had been rough. We went through the report and it went fine. It's not mind-reading, Binita. I, Jyoti, just watch a bit longer before I speak now. Sometimes I'm wrong. But waiting rarely hurts.

qa.q: What did Jyoti send the manager instead of presenting the report?
qa.a: A one-line message saying the report was ready whenever it suited her, no rush today.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling on noticing the manager's mood, and which cues were read?
qa.a: Jyoti felt cautious, sensing the manager was upset from the dropped laptop, the tight jaw and the unprompted "Fine".

qa.q: What could someone learn from Jyoti's approach?
qa.a: Notice tone and body cues, delay a request that isn't urgent, and offer an easy opening, while staying open to being wrong.

qa.q: What is it like for the manager to get a no-rush message after a rough call?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and respected, able to calm down first, which is why she came over later and explained.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a manager's mood and adjusting timing thoughtfully.
